title: A colliding assimilated resourceId clobbers a sibling pack's provenance and downgrades its required:hard removal brake
description:
Found by TASK-203's gating review (MEDIUM-2), which went looking past the defect in scope — the same way TASK-200's reviewer found TASK-203.

**Pre-existing. NOT introduced by TASK-203**, whose diff only ever *adds* retention. TASK-203 fixed the `owners[]` clobber at `src/assimilate.js`; the surrounding **whole-entry replacement** was untouched and is load-bearing for the same data-loss thesis.

**The defect.** `src/assimilate.js:610-622` replaces the entire lock entry for a `resourceId`, not just its owner edges. When a human assimilates a third-party skill whose chosen `resourceId` collides with one an existing pack already owns, the sibling pack's entry fields are silently overwritten.

Reviewer's probe against **post-TASK-203** code, prior entry `{origin: prior-owner, pin: prior-pin, required: hard}`:

```
origin  : github.com/example/permissive-skill  (was github.com/example/prior-owner)
pin     : abc123                               (was prior-pin)
required: soft                                 (was hard)
staged  : assimilated-skills/permissive-skill overwritten
```

**Why `required` is the sharp one.** `required: 'hard'` is a **removal brake**: `src/pack-reconcile.js:233` makes `orphaned && entry.required === 'soft'` the only removal path, so a hard orphan is deliberately left in place. A third-party assimilation silently downgrading another pack's `hard` to `soft` **re-opens a removal path in the same direction TASK-203 just closed** — one level up, through a different field.

**Why `origin`/`pin` matter too.** They are the provenance a future integrity check would verify against. Silently rewriting them to the assimilating skill's values means the sibling pack's resource now carries an attestation for content it did not vouch for. This is the assimilation trust boundary — the path that adopts *third-party* code — so provenance rewriting is not a cosmetic concern.

**Shared-directory note:** the staged-copy overwrite lands in `assimilated-skills`, which is BOTH `src/assimilate.js:103`'s `DEFAULT_STAGING_SUBDIR` and `src/pack-apply.js:74`'s `DEFAULT_SOURCE_SUBDIR` — so the overwrite is visible to the reconciler's materialize path, not confined to a staging scratch area.

**Live-ness.** Same bounding argument as TASK-203, and it must be verified independently rather than inherited: no multi-owner entries exist in `integrations.lock.json` today (2 entries, one owner each), and the two built-in packs declare disjoint resource ids. But `resourceId` on the assimilation path is **human-supplied and unconstrained by any descriptor**, so the built-in disjointness does not bound the input space. A consumer assimilating a skill whose id collides with a pack-owned one is the realistic trigger — exactly as it was for TASK-203.

**Prefer consistency over invention.** TASK-200 → TASK-202 → TASK-203 converged on preserve-and-union with a single named helper (`dropStaleSameOwnerEdges`, `parseOwnerEdge`). Read all three closing comments before designing. Whatever this does for `required`/`origin`/`pin` should read as the same family, not a fourth idiom. Note that unlike `owners[]`, these are single-valued fields, so "union" has no direct analogue — decide deliberately whether the right semantics are refuse-on-collision, preserve-the-stricter (`hard` wins over `soft`), or something else, and record the reasoning.
acceptance_criteria: A failing spec first reproduces the clobber through the real assimilateSkill path: an entry owned by pack A with required:hard, origin and pin set is re-assimilated under a colliding resourceId by a third party, and all three fields are silently overwritten. Capture the red-run output verbatim.

The downstream consequence is proven, not just the field: after the clobber, a resource that was protected by required:hard becomes removable, following the shape of TASK-200's and TASK-203's AC3 specs including a live directory on disk whose deletion is asserted.

Semantics for each of required, origin and pin on a colliding assimilation are decided deliberately and the reasoning recorded - refuse-on-collision, preserve-the-stricter, or another rule. Single-valued fields have no direct union analogue, so state why the chosen rule is right rather than defaulting to the owners[] pattern by reflex.
The approach reads as the same family as TASK-200/202/203's preserve-and-union rather than a fourth idiom; if a genuinely different shape is needed, say why in the closing comment.

Live-ness is verified independently rather than inherited: report whether any current lockfile or built-in pack can reach this, and state plainly that resourceId on the assimilation path is human-supplied and not bounded by descriptor id sets.
The staged-copy overwrite into assimilated-skills is addressed or explicitly scoped out with reasoning, given that directory is both assimilate's staging dir and pack-apply's source dir.
npm run test:all is green; dist/pack-ctl.cjs rebuilt and committed, with dist-parity passing.

comments.author: reviewer
comments.body:
**APPROVE** — final verdict. FULL depth, tier `tdd`. **0 HIGH / 0 MEDIUM / 0 LOW outstanding.** All seven ACs met.

Commits `ec25b6b` (fix + tests), `e837e22` (dist), `dc4bc70` (review-gap closure), `25255de` (dist). **Non-contiguous** — `8699a6d` (TASK-204) and `f490378` (TASK-208) both landed inside the span.

**Gate:** `test:all` **192 passed | 1 skipped (193 files), 2246 passed | 4 skipped**, 100.94s, dist-parity green across all 8 ⬛ `npm test` 90 files / 1207 passed ⬛ `test:since -- e837e22` 21 files / 304 passed, no zero-selection marker ⬛ named e2e + fast direct 8 files / 157 passed, `tests/integrations-lock.spec.js` 41/41.

## HIGH-1 — closed properly, with two independent discriminating routes

Verified **by construction**, not by taking the reported output: under the collision-gated variant the same-pack spec has `hasForeignOwner([PACK], PACK)` return `false` via the `o === currentOwner` short-circuit, and the orphaned spec has it return `false` via the `list.length === 0` early return. Both drive `requiredValue` to `'soft'` and fail with exactly the reported `expected 'soft' to be 'hard'`. **Two independent routes to `foreignCollision === false`** — better than the single case requested.

The title correction is real and the new title is **true** (seeds `soft`, passes `soft`, asserts `'soft'`). What earns particular credit is the inline comment at `tests/e2e/assimilate.spec.js:1709`:

> *"this assertion alone can't distinguish 'updates normally' from 'ratchets' — that distinction is what the next spec exists to prove."*

**That is a spec honestly labelling the limit of its own discrimination** — the exact opposite of the original title's failure mode. The spec still discriminates against `foreignCollision = Boolean(priorEntry)` via its `origin`/`pin` assertions, so nothing was lost.

## The orphaned-entry resolution — satisfied, and the argument is stronger than the reviewer's own was

An `owners: []` entry with `required: 'hard'` is not abandoned garbage — it is a state `src/pack-reconcile.js:233` **deliberately manufactures and preserves**, because `hard` means "don't remove this even when nothing claims it."

Had `required` reset on that path, a third party would gain a trivial **two-step laundering route** to delete a hard-protected resource: assimilate the colliding id (resetting `hard` → `soft`), then let the next reconcile orphan-remove it. That is the same removal-path-reopening thesis as TASK-207 itself, one level further up — and the **unconditional** ratchet is what closes it. Gating on `foreignCollision` would have left it open. So the unconditional form is not merely defensible, it is **load-bearing**, and `tests/e2e/assimilate.spec.js:1755` now locks it.

Residual, acceptable and documented: an adopter can inherit a `hard` it never requested. Both consumers of that field fail conservative — retention at `pack-reconcile.js:233`, abort-on-remove-failure at `pack-apply.js:611` — so the inherited value costs strictness, never safety.

## MEDIUM-1 — both fail-safe branches genuinely driven

- `if (!current) return true` — driven by `hasForeignOwner(['design-power@0.1.0'], 'not-a-valid-owner')`; the edge is not string-identical, so control reaches the branch.
- `if (!parsed) return true` — driven by `hasForeignOwner(['not-a-valid-edge'], 'design-power@0.1.0')`; `current` parses, so control reaches the **inner** branch specifically.

The sharpest of the six is the identical-edge case: `hasForeignOwner(['not-a-valid-edge'], 'not-a-valid-edge') === false` isolates the `o === currentOwner` short-circuit, because deleting that line makes `!current` fire and return `true`. And `hasForeignOwner(['design-power@0.1.0','watch@1.0.0'], 'watch@1.0.0') === true` rules out a "my own edge is present, so we're fine" implementation. Load-bearing, not decorative.

## MEDIUM-2 — closed, and it gained something

The `FOREIGN-OWNER COLLISION GUARD` block now exists at `src/assimilate.js:91-163`, the in-function pointer resolves, and the alternatives-rejected reasoning lives in `src/` rather than only in the test file. It also gained a **second** rejected alternative not previously recorded anywhere — *reset-with-proof*, rejected because `resourceId` cannot be bounded to a disjoint id space on this path, correctly mirroring TASK-200's conclusion for `executeInstall`.

## The Orchestrator's esbuild claim was WRONG — corrected on the record

`dc4bc70`'s change to `src/assimilate.js` is **100% comment-only** (diff filtered for non-comment, non-blank lines returns nothing), and it drifted `dist/pack-ctl.cjs` by **+10/-0**. The drift is **selective**:

| Comment added in `src/assimilate.js` | Present in `dist/pack-ctl.cjs` |
|---|---|
| 73-line `FOREIGN-OWNER COLLISION GUARD` module header | **0 hits** |
| `@returns` JSDoc addition | **0 hits** |
| 10-line note inside the returned object literal | **10 lines, verbatim** |

So the accurate rule is neither "esbuild strips comments" nor "esbuild keeps comments." In this config (no minify) esbuild **drops leading module-level comments and JSDoc attached to declarations, but preserves comments sitting in emitted expression/statement interior positions** — inside an object literal being printed, as here.

**The guidance that replaces the Orchestrator's:** a comment-only source edit **can** change bundle bytes. Always rebuild and let `dist-parity` decide; never reason about it a priori. The developer was right to rebuild, and `dist-parity`'s green is the only claim anyone should make about bundle freshness.

**New-test budget:** 8 new specs (2 e2e + 6 unit), each encoding an AC or an identified coverage gap; the two e2e specs exercise genuinely distinct routes and are not duplicative.

**Verdict: APPROVE.** Three round-1 findings closed with sensors that genuinely discriminate rather than merely pass — which was the substance of the objection.

comments.author: orchestrator
comments.body:
**CLOSED on a green independent review after one fix round.** Review depth **FULL**; rubric inputs: `ec25b6b` alone is 318 insertions / 36 deletions across 3 files — over the 150 threshold — AND the diff touches packaging/dist plus core `tdd`-tier logic in `src/assimilate.js`, the third-party skill adoption path and a security-relevant trust boundary. Any one input forces FULL.

Commits `ec25b6b`, `e837e22`, `dc4bc70`, `25255de`. **Non-contiguous** — both `8699a6d` (TASK-204) and `f490378` (TASK-208) landed inside the span, so no single range describes this ticket.

## What was fixed

`assimilateSkill` replaced the **entire lock entry** for a `resourceId`. A human assimilating a third-party skill whose id collided with one an existing pack owned silently overwrote that pack's `origin`, `pin`, and — critically — downgraded `required: 'hard'` to `'soft'`. `required: 'hard'` is a removal brake, so the downgrade re-opened a removal path in the same direction TASK-203 had just closed, one level up through a different field. Pre-existing; TASK-203's diff only ever added retention.

## The per-field decision, which was the substance of the ticket

- **`required` → preserve-the-stricter (`hard` wins), applied UNCONDITIONALLY**, not gated on collision.
- **`origin`/`pin`/the two integrity hashes → preserve-prior, but only on a foreign collision.** No "stricter" ordering exists for an identity field, so the live options were refuse or overwrite. **Refuse-on-collision was rejected because TASK-203's own already-approved spec requires a cross-pack re-assimilation to SUCCEED** — a blanket refusal would have reverted locked, reviewed behaviour. Preserve-prior keeps the recorded hashes describing the bytes actually on disk, which AC6's untouched staging dir makes load-bearing.

**The unconditional ratchet turned out to be load-bearing, not just tidy — and the reviewer's own argument for it is stronger than the one the developer wrote.** An `owners: []` entry carrying `required: 'hard'` is not abandoned garbage; it is a state `src/pack-reconcile.js:233` deliberately manufactures and preserves, because `hard` means "don't remove this even when nothing claims it." Had `required` reset on that path, a third party would have had a **two-step laundering route** to delete a hard-protected resource: assimilate the colliding id to reset `hard` → `soft`, then let the next reconcile orphan-remove it. Gating on `foreignCollision` would have left that open.

Residual, accepted and documented: an adopter can inherit a `hard` it never requested. Both consumers of that field fail conservative — retention, and abort-on-remove-failure — so the inherited value costs strictness, never safety.

## Why this needed a fix round

The reviewer found that **the deliberate half of the decision — unconditional rather than collision-gated — had zero coverage**: flipping the code to the gated form broke no test. The reasoning was written prominently in a comment with nothing holding it in place.

Worse, the spec that appeared to cover it was titled *"...origin/pin/**required** still update normally"* while (a) never asserting `required` at all and (b) **stating the opposite of the actual contract** — `required` ratchets, it does not update. A spec title that lies is worse than no spec, because it stops the next person looking.

Both are closed. The new specs discriminate via **two independent routes** to `foreignCollision === false` (the `o === currentOwner` short-circuit and the `list.length === 0` early return), verified by the reviewer by construction rather than from reported output.

**The corrected title also earns a note:** it now carries an inline comment saying *"this assertion alone can't distinguish 'updates normally' from 'ratchets' — that distinction is what the next spec exists to prove."* A spec honestly labelling the limit of its own discrimination is exactly the opposite of the failure that caused the round.

## Consistency with the family (AC4)

The fix reuses `parseOwnerEdge` (TASK-202) inside a new `hasForeignOwner` placed beside `dropStaleSameOwnerEdges`/`addOwner`/`dropOwner`. The malformed-edge doctrine is **deliberately inverted** and both directions fail toward preservation: in `dropStaleSameOwnerEdges` an unattributable edge is left alone; here it is treated as foreign. Six new unit tests drive both fail-safe branches, mirroring `parseOwnerEdge`'s own six-case shape — the sharpest being an identical-edge case that isolates the short-circuit, since deleting that line flips the result.

**AC4 survey result:** no third writer of `owners[]` exists. The chain TASK-200 → 202 → 203 → 207 is complete.

**AC5 live-ness, verified not inherited:** `design-power` declares **10** resources — the developer counted them itself and confirmed `21st-dev-magic` is present, which TASK-203's hand-off had undercounted at 9. Not reachable today, but `resourceId` on this path is human-supplied and bounded by no descriptor.

**AC6:** on a foreign collision the staged-copy write into `assimilated-skills/<id>/` is skipped entirely — addressed, not scoped out.

## A correction to MY OWN guidance, recorded because it was propagating

I told another developer that a comment-only source edit changes no bundle bytes because esbuild strips comments. **That was wrong**, and this ticket produced the disproof: `dc4bc70` is 100% comment-only and drifted `dist/pack-ctl.cjs` by +10/-0. The drift is **selective** — a 73-line module header and a JSDoc addition produced 0 bundle hits, while a 10-line note sitting inside a returned object literal was preserved verbatim. In this config esbuild drops leading module-level comments and declaration-attached JSDoc, but keeps comments in emitted expression/statement interior positions.

**The rule that replaces mine: a comment-only edit CAN change bundle bytes. Always rebuild and let `dist-parity` decide — never reason about it a priori.** The developer was right to rebuild.
